parent_reference.heading: 1. At a Glance
parent_reference.content:
- **Topic**: Chess Pieces
- **Difficulty**: Beginner
- **Typical age**: 6+
- **Estimated teaching time**: 10 min
- **Piece/concept type**: Concept
- **Prerequisites**: Chess Board (TOP-001)

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child can identify the six different types of chess pieces by name and sight.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- Child can correctly name a King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, and Pawn when shown.
- Child knows there are two armies: White and Black.
- Child understands they do not need to know how they move yet — just their names.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" Yes. This is a pure vocabulary lesson before getting into the complex movement rules.)*

---

parent_reference.heading: 2. Definition
parent_reference.content:
Chess pieces (or "men") are the physical objects moved on the chess board. There are 32 pieces in total, divided into two armies of 16 (one White, one Black). There are exactly six unique types of pieces in a chess army: King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, and Pawn.

---

parent_reference.heading: 3. Why It Matters
parent_reference.content:
Before a child can learn *how* a piece moves, they must know *what* it is. Trying to teach the names of the pieces at the exact same time as teaching how they move causes extreme cognitive overload for a young child. Separating "Piece Identification" into its own quick lesson ensures they have the vocabulary required for all future lessons. 

---

parent_reference.heading: 5. Parent Understands
parent_reference.content:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it.*

A standard chess set has 32 pieces. 
Each player controls an army of 16 pieces, consisting of:
- 1 King
- 1 Queen
- 2 Rooks
- 2 Bishops
- 2 Knights
- 8 Pawns

Pieces are often categorized. The Queen and Rooks are called **Major Pieces** (because they are very powerful). The Bishops and Knights are called **Minor Pieces** (because they are less powerful). Pawns are usually just called pawns.

---

parent_reference.heading: 6. How to Teach It
parent_reference.content:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — Introduce the Armies (2 mins)
Pour all 32 pieces onto the table in a messy pile.
> *"Look at all these! There are 32 pieces here. But they are divided into two teams. Can you separate them into the White army and the Black army?"*
Let them sort the pile by color.

### Step 2 — The Meet and Greet (5 mins)
Take one of each White piece and line them up. Point to them one by one.
> *"There are six different characters in our army. Let's meet them!"*
- Point to the **Pawn**: *"This is the Pawn. He's the little foot-soldier. You have 8 of these!"*
- Point to the **Knight**: *"This is the Knight. It looks like a horse!"*
- Point to the **Bishop**: *"This is the Bishop. He has a little cut in his tall hat."*
- Point to the **Rook**: *"This is the Rook. It looks like a castle tower."*
- Point to the **Queen**: *"This is the Queen. She has a crown with little points on it. She's the most powerful."*
- Point to the **King**: *"This is the King. He has a cross on top of his crown. He is the most important piece in the whole game."*

### Step 3 — Quiz Time (3 mins)
Mix the 6 pieces up. 
> *"Okay, close your eyes!"* (Mix them). *"Open! Point to the Rook! Point to the Bishop!"*

---

parent_reference.heading: 7. Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
parent_reference.content:
> **👑 The Royal Family Analogy**
> 
> Imagine the chess pieces are a real kingdom! The **King and Queen** are the rulers. The **Bishops** are their smart advisors who whisper in their ears. The **Knights** are the brave soldiers riding horses to protect them. The **Rooks** are the strong castle walls keeping everyone safe. And the **Pawns** are the loyal villagers and guards standing out in front of the castle!
>
> **Memory Trick:**
> **"The King wears a Cross, the Queen wears a Crown."** (This helps children tell the two tallest pieces apart).

---

parent_reference.heading: 8. Did You Know? 🎓
parent_reference.content:
The "Rook" looks like a castle tower, but the word actually comes from the ancient Persian word "Rukh," which meant "Chariot"! Hundreds of years ago, before chess came to Europe, people didn't play with castles — they played with fast-moving war chariots.

---

parent_reference.heading: 9. Board Diagram 1 — Basic Concept
parent_reference.content:
**The 6 Types of Pieces**

![DGM-007-01 All Pieces](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-007/DGM-007-01_All_Pieces.svg)
*From left to right: King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, Pawn. Learning to tell them apart by silhouette is a core chess skill.*

---

parent_reference.heading: 10. How It Works
parent_reference.content:
Every piece has a unique way of moving, a unique value, and a unique role in the army. However, you do NOT need to teach movement today. Today is just about identification. 

---

parent_reference.heading: 11. Board Diagram 2 — Practical Example
parent_reference.content:
**White Army vs Black Army**

![DGM-007-02 Armies](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-007/DGM-007-02_Armies.svg)
*Both armies have the exact same pieces. The White pieces always move first in a game of chess.*

---

parent_reference.heading: 12. Real Game Example
parent_reference.content:
![DGM-007-03 Piece Families](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-007/DGM-007-03_Piece_Families.svg)
As players get better, they group pieces into families. The Queen and Rook are "Major Pieces." The Bishop and Knight are "Minor Pieces." When grandmasters talk about a game, they might say, "I traded a minor piece for a major piece," meaning they gave up a Knight to capture a Rook!

---

parent_reference.heading: 13. Common Mistakes
parent_reference.content:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Confusing the King and Queen** — They are both tall. The King has a cross; the Queen has a jagged crown.
- ❌ **Calling the Knight a "Horse"** — It's okay at first, but gently correct them to "Knight."
- ❌ **Calling the Rook a "Castle"** — Same as above. The piece is a Rook. ("Castling" is a special move they will learn later).

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Teaching movement too early** — Do not explain how the pieces move during this lesson. If they ask, say: "That's a secret for our next lesson!" Teaching movement right now causes confusion.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If your child keeps calling the Knight a "horse," don't get frustrated. Say, "You're right, it looks exactly like a horse! But its secret chess name is a Knight."

---

parent_reference.heading: 14. Teaching Notes
parent_reference.content:
- **Let them touch:** Children learn through tactile feedback. Let them hold the pieces, feel the cross on the King, and trace the cut on the Bishop's hat.
- **Signs they understand:** You can point to any piece in the box and they can name it instantly.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> To help them distinguish the Bishop from the Pawn (which sometimes look similar in cheap plastic sets), point out that the Bishop is taller and always has a little slit/cut in its headpiece.

---

parent_reference.heading: 15. Parent FAQ
parent_reference.content:
**Q: Do I need to teach them how much each piece is worth (points) today?**
A: No. Piece values (TOP-014) come much later, after they understand how the pieces actually move. Today is strictly about names and shapes.

**Q: My child already knows the names. Should I skip this?**
A: You can breeze through it, but do a quick check. Ensure they know the difference between the King and Queen, and ensure they are using the proper names (Rook, not Castle).

**Q: Why does White always go first?**
A: It's just a standardized rule made in the 1800s to make tournaments fair and easy to record. Before that, players would flip a coin to see who moved first, regardless of color!

---

parent_reference.heading: 16. Practice Together
parent_reference.content:
### 🎒 The Grab Bag
Put one of each piece inside a small bag (or under a towel). Ask your child to reach in without looking. Tell them: "Pull out the Knight!" They have to feel the shapes with their fingers to find the right piece. This is fantastic for tactile memory.

### 🕵️‍♂️ Line Up
Give your child 6 random pieces. Ask them to line them up from shortest to tallest. (Usually: Pawn, Knight, Bishop, Rook, Queen, King). This helps them notice the physical differences.

---

parent_reference.heading: 17. Coach Challenge ⭐
parent_reference.content:
### 🏆 The Missing Piece
**Challenge your child:**
> "I am going to put all 6 pieces on the table. Then you close your eyes, and I will steal one! Let's see if you can figure out who is missing."

**Rules:**
1. Place 1 King, 1 Queen, 1 Rook, 1 Bishop, 1 Knight, and 1 Pawn on the board.
2. The child closes their eyes.
3. You remove one piece and hide it behind your back.
4. They open their eyes and guess who is missing!
5. Swap roles — let them steal a piece from you!

---

parent_reference.heading: 18. Try It Yourself
parent_reference.content:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
Look at the two tallest pieces. Which one has a cross on top?
*Answer: The King!*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
Look at the diagram below. Which piece is missing from this lineup?
![DGM-007-04 Puzzle](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-007/DGM-007-04_Puzzle.svg)
*Answer: The Bishop is missing.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
![DGM-007-05 Puzzle Solution](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-007/DGM-007-05_Puzzle_Solution.svg)
If you count all the Pawns on BOTH teams, how many Pawns are there in the whole game?
*Answer: 16! (8 White pawns + 8 Black pawns).*

---

parent_reference.content:

parent_reference.heading: 21. Parent Confidence Check ✅
parent_reference.content:
- [ ] Do I know the difference between a major piece and a minor piece?
- [ ] Can my child name all 6 pieces?
- [ ] Can my child tell the King and Queen apart?
- [ ] Does my child know to call it a "Rook" instead of a "Castle"?
- [ ] Does my child know to call it a "Knight" instead of a "Horse"?

**✅ If most answers are "Yes":** Congratulations — your child has the vocabulary to learn movement! Move on to **King (TOP-008)** or **Rook (TOP-010)**.
**🔄 If several answers are "No":** Play "The Grab Bag" in Section 16 to build piece familiarity.

> Imagine the chess pieces are a real kingdom! The **King and Queen** are the rulers. The **Bishops** are their smart advisors who whisper in their ears. The **Knights** are the brave soldiers riding horses to protect them. The **Rooks** are the strong castle walls keeping everyone safe. And the **Pawns** are the loyal villagers and guards standing out in front of the castle!
>
> **Memory Trick:**
> **"The King wears a Cross, the Queen wears a Crown."** (This helps children tell the two tallest pieces apart).

guide_sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
guide_sections.text: The "Rook" looks like a castle tower, but the word actually comes from the ancient Persian word "Rukh," which meant "Chariot"! Hundreds of years ago, before chess came to Europe, people didn't play with castles — they played with fast-moving war chariots.

guide_sections.title: Real Game Example
guide_sections.text: As players get better, they group pieces into families. The Queen and Rook are "Major Pieces." The Bishop and Knight are "Minor Pieces." When grandmasters talk about a game, they might say, "I traded a minor piece for a major piece," meaning they gave up a Knight to capture a Rook!

guide_sections.title: Common Mistakes
guide_sections.text:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Confusing the King and Queen** — They are both tall. The King has a cross; the Queen has a jagged crown.
- ❌ **Calling the Knight a "Horse"** — It's okay at first, but gently correct them to "Knight."
- ❌ **Calling the Rook a "Castle"** — Same as above. The piece is a Rook. ("Castling" is a special move they will learn later).

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Teaching movement too early** — Do not explain how the pieces move during this lesson. If they ask, say: "That's a secret for our next lesson!" Teaching movement right now causes confusion.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If your child keeps calling the Knight a "horse," don't get frustrated. Say, "You're right, it looks exactly like a horse! But its secret chess name is a Knight."

guide_sections.title: Teaching Notes
guide_sections.text:
- **Let them touch:** Children learn through tactile feedback. Let them hold the pieces, feel the cross on the King, and trace the cut on the Bishop's hat.
- **Signs they understand:** You can point to any piece in the box and they can name it instantly.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> To help them distinguish the Bishop from the Pawn (which sometimes look similar in cheap plastic sets), point out that the Bishop is taller and always has a little slit/cut in its headpiece.

guide_sections.title: Parent FAQ
guide_sections.text:
**Q: Do I need to teach them how much each piece is worth (points) today?**
A: No. Piece values (TOP-014) come much later, after they understand how the pieces actually move. Today is strictly about names and shapes.

**Q: My child already knows the names. Should I skip this?**
A: You can breeze through it, but do a quick check. Ensure they know the difference between the King and Queen, and ensure they are using the proper names (Rook, not Castle).

**Q: Why does White always go first?**
A: It's just a standardized rule made in the 1800s to make tournaments fair and easy to record. Before that, players would flip a coin to see who moved first, regardless of color!

guide_sections.title: Practice Together
guide_sections.text:
### 🎒 The Grab Bag
Put one of each piece inside a small bag (or under a towel). Ask your child to reach in without looking. Tell them: "Pull out the Knight!" They have to feel the shapes with their fingers to find the right piece. This is fantastic for tactile memory.

### 🕵️‍♂️ Line Up
Give your child 6 random pieces. Ask them to line them up from shortest to tallest. (Usually: Pawn, Knight, Bishop, Rook, Queen, King). This helps them notice the physical differences.

guide_sections.title: Coach Challenge ⭐
guide_sections.text:
### 🏆 The Missing Piece
**Challenge your child:**
> "I am going to put all 6 pieces on the table. Then you close your eyes, and I will steal one! Let's see if you can figure out who is missing."

**Rules:**
1. Place 1 King, 1 Queen, 1 Rook, 1 Bishop, 1 Knight, and 1 Pawn on the board.
2. The child closes their eyes.
3. You remove one piece and hide it behind your back.
4. They open their eyes and guess who is missing!
5. Swap roles — let them steal a piece from you!

guide_sections.title: Try It Yourself
guide_sections.text:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
Look at the two tallest pieces. Which one has a cross on top?
*Answer: The King!*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
Look at the diagram below. Which piece is missing from this lineup?

*Answer: The Bishop is missing.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)

If you count all the Pawns on BOTH teams, how many Pawns are there in the whole game?
*Answer: 16! (8 White pawns + 8 Black pawns).*

**🎯 Today's Goal:**
Your child can identify the six different types of chess pieces by name and sight.

**✅ Lesson Success Criteria:**
- Child can correctly name a King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, and Pawn when shown.
- Child knows there are two armies: White and Black.
- Child understands they do not need to know how they move yet — just their names.

*(Purpose: "Can I teach this today?" Yes. This is a pure vocabulary lesson before getting into the complex movement rules.)*

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Chess pieces (or "men") are the physical objects moved on the chess board. There are 32 pieces in total, divided into two armies of 16 (one White, one Black). There are exactly six unique types of pieces in a chess army: King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, and Pawn.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.text: Before a child can learn *how* a piece moves, they must know *what* it is. Trying to teach the names of the pieces at the exact same time as teaching how they move causes extreme cognitive overload for a young child. Separating "Piece Identification" into its own quick lesson ensures they have the vocabulary required for all future lessons.

sections.title: Parent Understands
sections.text:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it.*

A standard chess set has 32 pieces. 
Each player controls an army of 16 pieces, consisting of:
- 1 King
- 1 Queen
- 2 Rooks
- 2 Bishops
- 2 Knights
- 8 Pawns

Pieces are often categorized. The Queen and Rooks are called **Major Pieces** (because they are very powerful). The Bishops and Knights are called **Minor Pieces** (because they are less powerful). Pawns are usually just called pawns.

sections.title: How to Teach It
sections.text:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — Introduce the Armies (2 mins)
Pour all 32 pieces onto the table in a messy pile.
> *"Look at all these! There are 32 pieces here. But they are divided into two teams. Can you separate them into the White army and the Black army?"*
Let them sort the pile by color.

### Step 2 — The Meet and Greet (5 mins)
Take one of each White piece and line them up. Point to them one by one.
> *"There are six different characters in our army. Let's meet them!"*
- Point to the **Pawn**: *"This is the Pawn. He's the little foot-soldier. You have 8 of these!"*
- Point to the **Knight**: *"This is the Knight. It looks like a horse!"*
- Point to the **Bishop**: *"This is the Bishop. He has a little cut in his tall hat."*
- Point to the **Rook**: *"This is the Rook. It looks like a castle tower."*
- Point to the **Queen**: *"This is the Queen. She has a crown with little points on it. She's the most powerful."*
- Point to the **King**: *"This is the King. He has a cross on top of his crown. He is the most important piece in the whole game."*

### Step 3 — Quiz Time (3 mins)
Mix the 6 pieces up. 
> *"Okay, close your eyes!"* (Mix them). *"Open! Point to the Rook! Point to the Bishop!"*
